La phrase conditionnelle relie une condition (proposition en if) et sa conséquence. Le temps employé dans la proposition en if indique si l'hypothèse est réelle, imaginaire ou passée.

TypeProposition en ifPrincipaleExemple
vérité généraleprésentprésentIf you burn coal, you release CO₂.
hypothèse réaliste (futur possible)présentwill + BVIf the rocket lands safely, they will reuse it.
hypothèse imaginaire (présent ou futur peu probable)prétéritwould + BVIf I went to Scotland, I would visit Whitelee.
hypothèse sur le passé (irréel du passé)past perfectwould have + participe passéIf Watt had not improved the engine, the revolution would have been slower.
  • Jamais de will ni de would dans la proposition en if : If it rains tomorrow… (pas if it will rain).
  • Avec be, la langue soignée emploie were à toutes les personnes : If I were a scientist, I would study genes.
  • La virgule n'est nécessaire que si la proposition en if vient en premier.
  • could ou might peuvent remplacer would : If we built more turbines, we could close the last power stations.

Unless, as long as, provided that

unless = if… not (à moins que) : Unless we act now, some orbits will become unusable. = If we don't act now… Le verbe après unless est affirmatif.

as long as / provided (that) = à condition que : Space tourism is acceptable as long as it does not pollute. Ces conjonctions suivent les mêmes règles de temps que if.

Attention

If (si, condition) et whether (si, alternative dans une question indirecte) ne sont pas interchangeables dans une conditionnelle : I'll go if you go, mais I don't know whether he'll come.

sections.titre: Grammar: inversion and modals of probability
sections.html:
L'hypothèse par inversion

Dans une langue soutenue, on peut supprimer if et placer l'auxiliaire avant le sujet :

  • If she had known… → Had she known the risks, she would have refused.
  • If I were in charge… → Were I in charge, I would ban space tourism.
  • If you should need help… → Should you need help, contact the lab.

La négation se place après le sujet : Had Watt not improved the engine, … (jamais Hadn't Watt… dans cette structure).

Les modaux de probabilité

Ils expriment le degré de certitude de celui qui parle.

CertitudeSur le présent ou le futurSur le passé
quasi-certitudemust + BV : He must be a bioethicist.must have + participe passé : The debris must have hit the satellite.
possibilitémay / might / could + BV : Space-mining might become profitable.may / might / could have + participe passé : The engineers might have made a mistake.
impossibilitécan't / couldn't + BV : That can't be true.can't / couldn't have + participe passé : He can't have seen the launch: he was in London.
forte probabilité (futur)will probably / be likely to : Prices are likely to soar.was / were likely to

On peut aussi nuancer avec des adverbes : perhaps, maybe, probably, certainly, undoubtedly.

Attention

Le contraire de must (probabilité) est can't, pas mustn't : It can't be Dolly (ce ne peut pas être Dolly). Mustn't exprime une interdiction (chapitre 5).

Les connecteurs donnent sa logique à un argument. Repère leur sens et leur construction.

SensConnecteursExemple
additionmoreover, furthermore, besides, in addition, what's moreWind power is clean. Moreover, it creates jobs.
illustrationfor instance, for example, such as, likerenewable sources such as wind and tides
causebecause, since, as, because of + nom, due to + nomLaunches are cheaper because of reusable rockets.
conséquenceso, therefore, consequently, as a result, thusOil will run out; therefore, we must invest in wind.
oppositionbut, however, whereas, while, on the contrary, on the one hand… on the other handCoal pollutes, whereas wind is clean.
concessionalthough, even though, though, yet, despite / in spite of + nom ou V-ing, neverthelessAlthough the treaty exists, the rules on space-mining are unclear.
conclusionto sum up, all in all, all things considered, in conclusionAll things considered, the benefits outweigh the risks.

Construction

  • although, even though, whereas, because + sujet + verbe : Although it is expensive, gene therapy saves lives.
  • despite, in spite of, because of, due to + nom ou V-ing : Despite the cost, the project went ahead. In spite of being expensive, …
  • however, moreover, therefore, nevertheless en tête de phrase, suivis d'une virgule : However, critics disagree.
Attention

Despite ne prend jamais of : despite the risks (ou in spite of the risks). Et even if (même si, hypothèse) n'a pas le sens de even though (bien que, fait réel).

chapitres.a_retenir:
• Le traité de l'espace (1967) fait de l'espace « l'apanage de l'humanité » : aucun État ne peut s'approprier la Lune. Les entreprises privées (SpaceX, fusées réutilisables, tourisme spatial) et l'exploitation des ressources posent de nouvelles questions, comme les débris spatiaux.
  • L'Écosse est passée du charbon et de la machine de James Watt (1769) au pétrole de la mer du Nord (1970), puis à l'éolien (Whitelee, Hywind, Seagreen), avec l'objectif de neutralité carbone en 2045.
  • Frankenstein (1818) interroge la responsabilité du savant ; l'eugénisme a conduit à des stérilisations forcées ; aujourd'hui, Dolly (1996), le génome humain et la thérapie génique relancent le débat sur l'enhancement.
  • Conditionnelles : if + présent → will ; if + prétérit → would ; if + past perfect → would have + participe passé ; jamais will / would après if ; unless = if not.
  • Inversion : Had she known…, Were I…, Should you… ; modaux de probabilité : must (quasi sûr), may / might / could (possible), can't (impossible), + have + participe passé pour le passé.
  • Connecteurs : although + proposition, despite + nom ou V-ing ; however, moreover, therefore en tête de phrase.

chapitres.chapeau: The English-speaking world invented the national park, but it also created the Dust Bowl. Poets and painters have celebrated nature as something sacred, while storms and fires remind us how fragile we are. Dans ce chapitre, tu étudies comment les sociétés anglophones protègent la nature, l'affrontent et la célèbrent, et tu apprends à exprimer l'obligation et la permission, à dire ce que l'on fait faire et à employer des phrasal verbs.

sections.html:
Le parc national est une invention américaine, reprise dans le monde entier. Lis le texte et repère les dates clés, puis les tensions entre protection et fréquentation.

The first national park

On 1 March 1872, President Ulysses S. Grant signed a law creating Yellowstone National Park, in the American West: it was the first national park in the world. Its geysers, hot springs and wildlife were to be preserved "for the benefit and enjoyment of the people". In 1916, the US government created the National Park Service to manage the growing number of parks.

John Muir, the wilderness prophet

John Muir, born in Scotland in 1838, emigrated to the United States as a child. He fell in love with the Sierra Nevada mountains of California and spent his life defending them. Thanks partly to his articles, Yosemite became a national park in 1890, and in 1892 he founded the Sierra Club, one of the first environmental organisations. In 1903, he went camping in Yosemite with President Theodore Roosevelt, who later protected millions of acres of public land.

Across the English-speaking world

Canada created its first national park at Banff, in the Rocky Mountains, in 1885. In Britain, the fight was about access: in 1932, hundreds of walkers took part in a "mass trespass" on Kinder Scout to demand the right to walk on private moorland. The Peak District became the first British national park in 1951.

Paradise lost?

National parks also have a darker side. Many were created on land where Native peoples had lived for thousands of years, and these peoples were forced to leave. Today, millions of visitors every year cause traffic jams, pollution and erosion. Rangers ask visitors to follow the "Leave No Trace" principles: you must take your rubbish home, you mustn't feed the animals, and you have to stay on the trails.

Sécheresses, ouragans, incendies : face aux événements extrêmes, les sociétés révèlent leurs fragilités et leurs capacités d'adaptation. Lis le texte et repère, pour chaque catastrophe, une cause humaine et une réponse.

The Dust Bowl

In the 1930s, the southern Great Plains of the United States were hit by years of drought. Farmers had ploughed up the native grasses that held the soil in place, so the wind blew the dry earth away in gigantic dust storms. On "Black Sunday", 14 April 1935, a black cloud turned day into night. Hundreds of thousands of people left the region, many of them for California. John Steinbeck told their story in The Grapes of Wrath (1939), and the government created a service to teach farmers how to protect the soil.

Hurricane Katrina

On 29 August 2005, Hurricane Katrina hit the coast of Louisiana and Mississippi. In New Orleans, the levees that protected the city broke and about 80 % of the city was flooded. More than 1,800 people died. The slow response of the authorities was strongly criticised, especially because the poorest neighbourhoods, often Black neighbourhoods, suffered most. The city later rebuilt and strengthened its flood defences.

Australia's Black Summer

During the summer of 2019-2020, huge bushfires burned millions of hectares of forest in south-eastern Australia. According to a WWF study, nearly three billion animals were killed or displaced. Scientists explained that climate change makes such fires more frequent and more intense. Since then, Australians have been learning to live with fire: early warnings, fire bans and the revival of Aboriginal "cool burning", a traditional practice of small controlled fires that reduces fuel on the ground.

Méthode : exprimer des sentiments

I was appalled by… / I find it heartbreaking that… / It is shocking that… / I can't help feeling sorry for… / What strikes me is…

sections.titre: Sacred nature in art and fiction
sections.html:
Pour certains artistes et certains peuples, la nature n'est pas seulement belle : elle est sacrée. Lis le texte et repère comment chaque œuvre ou chaque décision exprime ce lien.

The Romantic poets

At the beginning of the 19th century, English Romantic poets turned to nature as a source of emotion and spiritual truth. In I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud (1807), William Wordsworth describes a host of golden daffodils beside a lake in the Lake District; long afterwards, the memory of the flowers still fills his heart with pleasure. For the Romantics, nature could heal the soul.

Walden

In 1845, the American writer Henry David Thoreau built a small cabin in the woods near Walden Pond, in Massachusetts, and lived there for about two years. In Walden (1854), he explains that he wanted to live simply and "deliberately", far from the noise of modern society. His book inspired generations of environmentalists.

Painting the wilderness

From the 1820s, a group of American painters known as the Hudson River School, led by Thomas Cole, painted vast landscapes of mountains, rivers and forests. Their wilderness looks grand and almost divine, a kind of natural cathedral. A century later, the photographer Ansel Adams captured Yosemite in black and white, and his pictures helped to defend the parks.

A river with rights

For the Māori people of New Zealand, nature is linked to their ancestors. For the Whanganui iwi (tribe), the Whanganui River is an ancestor: "I am the river, and the river is me," says a traditional saying. In 2017, after a struggle of more than a century, New Zealand's Parliament recognised the river as a legal person, with its own rights and two guardians to speak for it.

Prononciation

Les consonnes affriquées /ʧ/ et /ʤ/ : change, nature, future /ˈfjuːʧə/ ; jungle, energy, damage /ˈdæmɪʤ/. Lettre muette : le l de calm, walk, half ; le w de wreck, wrong.

L'obligation

  • must + BV : obligation imposée par celui qui parle, ou règle écrite : You must stay on the trails.
  • have to + BV : obligation extérieure (règlement, circonstances) ; se conjugue à tous les temps : Visitors have to buy a pass. In 2005, thousands of people had to leave their homes. You will have to wait.
  • should / ought to + BV : conseil, devoir moral : We should protect wetlands. We ought to respect the land.
  • had better + BV : conseil pressant (sinon…) : You'd better take water with you.
  • shall : dans les textes juridiques, obligation : Visitors shall not enter this area. ; dans une question, une proposition : Shall we go?

Interdiction ou absence d'obligation ?

FormeSensExemple
mustn't + BVinterdiction (il ne faut pas)You mustn't feed the bears.
don't have to / needn't + BVabsence d'obligation (ce n'est pas la peine)You don't have to pay: entry is free.
be not allowed to / can'tinterdiction (pas le droit)You are not allowed to camp here.

La permission

can / may (plus formel) / be allowed to (à tous les temps) : You can fish in this lake. May I take a photo? In the 1930s, walkers were not allowed to cross private moorland. Demander poliment : Could I…? Would you mind if I opened the window?

La capacité

can (présent), could (passé, capacité générale), be able to (tous les temps, et réussite ponctuelle dans le passé) : Bears can run fast. After the flood, they were able to rebuild. One day we will be able to predict fires better.

Attention

Les modaux (must, can, should) n'ont ni -s, ni to après eux, ni futur : he must go, you will have to go (et non will must). « J'ai dû partir » se dit I had to leave.

Faire faire : make, let, have, get

StructureSensExemple
make + sb + BVobliger, faire faire (contrainte ou effet)The storm made the farmers leave. His death made me cry.
let + sb + BVlaisser, permettreThe rangers let us camp near the lake.
have + sb + BVfaire faire (service, demande)The park had volunteers plant trees.
get + sb + to + BVconvaincre qqn de faireMuir got the president to protect the land.
have / get + objet + participe passéfaire faire qqch par qqn (on ne dit pas qui)They had their house rebuilt. She got her roof repaired.

Au passif, make prend to : The farmers were made to leave. Let n'a pas de passif : on emploie be allowed to.

Les structures résultatives

L'anglais peut exprimer en une seule proposition une action et son résultat : verbe + complément + adjectif ou particule de résultat.

  • He watered the roses flat. (il a arrosé les roses, si bien qu'elles se sont couchées)
  • The wind blew the door open. (le vent a ouvert la porte en soufflant)
  • The fire burned the forest down. (l'incendie a réduit la forêt en cendres)
  • She painted the cabin green.

Le français traduit souvent le résultat par le verbe et la manière par un complément : He kicked the door open = il a ouvert la porte d'un coup de pied.

sections.titre: Grammar: phrasal verbs and the gerund
sections.html:
Les phrasal verbs

Un phrasal verb associe un verbe et une particule (up, down, out, off, away…) ; le sens n'est pas toujours la somme des deux.

Phrasal verbSensExemple
set upcréer, fonderMuir set up the Sierra Club.
cut downabattre (des arbres) ; réduireThey cut down the forest. Cut down on plastic!
run out ofmanquer de, être à court deThe farmers ran out of water.
wipe outanéantir, rayer de la carteThe fires wiped out entire species.
put outéteindre (un feu)Firefighters put out the fire.
look afters'occuper deRangers look after the park.
give upabandonner, renoncer àMany farmers gave up their land.
carry oncontinuerCarry on walking until the lake.
figure outcomprendre, trouverScientists are trying to figure out why.
throw awayjeterDon't throw away your rubbish here.

Avec un complément pronom, la particule se place après le pronom : They put it out (et non put out it). Avec un nom, les deux ordres sont possibles : put out the fire / put the fire out.

Un pronom réfléchi peut s'insérer : She pulled herself together (elle s'est ressaisie). They looked after themselves in the wild.

Le gérondif (V-ing)

  • sujet : Protecting wildlife is everyone's business.
  • après certains verbes : enjoy, avoid, stop, keep, mind, can't stand, finish, suggest : We enjoyed hiking. Avoid feeding the animals.
  • après une préposition : before leaving, without making noise, interested in protecting, et après look forward to : I'm looking forward to visiting Banff.
Attention

Stop doing = arrêter de faire ; stop to do = s'arrêter pour faire. Remember doing = se souvenir d'avoir fait ; remember to do = penser à faire.

• Yellowstone (1872) est le premier parc national du monde ; John Muir a défendu Yosemite et fondé le Sierra Club (1892) ; Banff (1885) et le Peak District (1951) ont suivi. Les parcs ont aussi chassé des peuples autochtones et souffrent de la surfréquentation.
  • Face aux extrêmes : le Dust Bowl des années 1930 (The Grapes of Wrath), l'ouragan Katrina (2005) à La Nouvelle-Orléans, le Black Summer australien (2019-2020) ; les sociétés s'adaptent (digues, alertes, brûlages traditionnels).
  • La nature sacralisée : Wordsworth et les romantiques, Walden de Thoreau, la Hudson River School ; en 2017, le fleuve Whanganui est devenu une personne juridique.
  • must / have to : obligation ; mustn't : interdiction ; don't have to : absence d'obligation ; be allowed to : permission ; be able to : capacité à tous les temps.
  • make / let / have + sb + BV ; get sb to + BV ; have sth done ; résultatives : The wind blew the door open.
  • Phrasal verbs : set up, cut down, run out of, wipe out, put out, look after ; pronom avant la particule (put it out). Gérondif : sujet, après enjoy, avoid et après une préposition (look forward to + V-ing).

chapitres.resume: Axe 6 (obligatoire), Les aires anglophones américaines : les Caraïbes, Porto Rico et la question du 51e État, Vancouver et Seattle. Grammaire : adjectifs composés, groupe nominal et distributifs ; wish et le regret ; questions en How, question tags et réponses courtes.
chapitres.chapeau: From the islands of the Caribbean to the rainy coast of the Pacific Northwest, the Americas are full of places where English meets other languages and cultures. Music, money, tourists and migrants travel in every direction, but not always on equal terms. Dans ce chapitre, tu découvres les Caraïbes anglophones, Porto Rico et deux villes voisines, Vancouver et Seattle, et tu apprends à construire des groupes nominaux précis, à exprimer un regret et à poser toutes sortes de questions.
objectifs: situer les Caraïbes anglophones et présenter leur influence culturelle dans le monde ;
expliquer le statut de Porto Rico et le débat sur le « 51e État » ;
comparer Vancouver et Seattle, deux villes voisines de part et d'autre d'une frontière ;
repérer des différences entre l'anglais britannique et l'anglais américain ;
construire des adjectifs composés et des groupes nominaux complexes, et employer les distributifs ;
exprimer un souhait ou un regret avec wish et if only ;
poser des questions en How et employer les question tags et les réponses courtes.

sections.html:
Les Caraïbes anglophones sont petites par la taille, mais immenses par leur influence. Lis le texte et repère ce que la région a reçu du monde, et ce qu'elle lui a donné.

From colonies to nations

For centuries, the islands of the Caribbean were European colonies where enslaved Africans were forced to work on sugar plantations. After the abolition of slavery in the British Empire in the 1830s, workers also came from India and China. In the 20th century, the British colonies became independent: Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago in 1962, Barbados in 1966. In 2021, Barbados went further and became a republic, replacing the British monarch with its own president.

In 1973, several of these countries founded the Caribbean Community, CARICOM, to cooperate on trade, education and health. Today it has fifteen full members.

A small region, a big voice

Caribbean culture travels far. Reggae, born in Jamaica in the late 1960s and made famous by Bob Marley, was added to UNESCO's list of the intangible cultural heritage of humanity in 2018. The steelpan and calypso come from Trinidad, whose carnival inspired carnivals in London, Toronto and New York. The poet Derek Walcott, born on the island of Saint Lucia in 1930, received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1992; in his long poem Omeros, he retells Homer's epic with Caribbean fishermen.

Unequal exchanges

The exchanges are not always equal. Many economies depend on tourism, especially on cruise ships from North America, and much of the money leaves the islands again. Hurricanes regularly destroy homes and roads. Many young graduates leave for the United States, Canada or Britain, and the Jamaican diaspora is now very large. Their families at home often depend on the money they send back.

Définition

Une diaspora est l'ensemble des membres d'un peuple dispersés hors de leur pays d'origine. Les envois d'argent des émigrés à leur famille s'appellent les remittances.

Porto Rico appartient aux États-Unis sans en être un État. Lis le texte et repère les étapes de cette relation, puis les trois options en débat.

An American territory

Puerto Rico, an island in the Caribbean, was a Spanish colony for four centuries. In 1898, after the Spanish-American War, Spain ceded it to the United States. In 1917, the Jones Act made Puerto Ricans US citizens. Since 1952, the island has been a Commonwealth (in Spanish, Estado Libre Asociado): it has its own constitution and governor, but it remains under the authority of the US Congress.

Citizens, but not quite

About 3.2 million people live on the island. Puerto Ricans can travel and work freely in the fifty states, and they serve in the US army. However, as long as they live on the island, they cannot vote in presidential elections, and they are represented in Congress by a single Resident Commissioner who cannot vote on final laws. Spanish and English are both official languages, but Spanish is the language of daily life for most people.

Three possible futures

Puerto Ricans are divided. Some want the island to become the 51st state of the United States, with full rights. Others prefer to keep the current status, which protects their Spanish-speaking identity. A minority want independence. In several non-binding referendums, most recently in 2020 and 2024, a majority of voters chose statehood, but only the US Congress can admit a new state, and it has never done so.

In September 2017, Hurricane Maria devastated the island and left most residents without electricity for months. The official death toll was later estimated at about 3,000. Many Puerto Ricans felt that they had been treated like second-class citizens, and tens of thousands left for the mainland: today more Puerto Ricans live in the fifty states than on the island.

sections.titre: Vancouver and Seattle: two cities, one region
sections.html:
Deux villes séparées par une frontière, mais unies par une même région : lis le texte et compare Vancouver et Seattle point par point (histoire, économie, culture).

Cascadia

Vancouver, in the Canadian province of British Columbia, and Seattle, in the US state of Washington, are only about 200 kilometres apart. Both stand on the Pacific coast, between the ocean and the mountains, in a green and rainy region that some people call Cascadia. Both were built on the lands of the Coast Salish peoples; Seattle is even named after a Duwamish and Suquamish chief, Si'ahl.

Two cities, two stories

Vancouver became a city in 1886, when the Canadian Pacific Railway arrived, and was named after the British navigator George Vancouver. Today it is Canada's largest port and one of the most multicultural cities in the country, with large Chinese and South Asian communities. It hosted the Expo 86 world's fair and the 2010 Winter Olympics, and its film industry has earned it the nickname "Hollywood North".

Seattle grew with the timber trade and the Klondike gold rush of the 1890s. Its symbol, the Space Needle, was built for the 1962 World's Fair. The city is the birthplace of Boeing (1916) and the home of Amazon and Starbucks, while Microsoft is based nearby. In the 1990s, it gave the world grunge music.

Cooperation and rivalry

Every day, workers, students and tourists cross the border at the Peace Arch, a monument built in 1921 to celebrate friendship between the two countries. The two cities cooperate on technology and research, and both hosted matches of the 2026 FIFA World Cup. But they are also rivals: their football teams, the Whitecaps and the Sounders, compete every year for the Cascadia Cup. And the American pull is strong: many Canadian tech workers are attracted by higher salaries in Seattle, while some Americans move north for a calmer life.

Méthode : comparer deux villes

Both cities are… / Neither city is… / Vancouver is bigger than…, whereas Seattle… / Like Vancouver, Seattle… / Unlike Seattle, Vancouver…

Accents

Reconnaître un accent aide à situer un document. L'anglais américain prononce le r final (car /kɑːr/), le britannique standard non (/kɑː/) ; le t entre deux voyelles ressemble à un /d/ rapide en américain (water, city). L'anglais jamaïcain et le patois jamaïcain ont leur propre rythme et leur vocabulaire.

sections.titre: Grammar: compound adjectives, noun groups, distributives
sections.html:
Les adjectifs composés

On les forme avec un trait d'union. Ils se placent devant le nom et restent invariables : le nom qu'ils contiennent ne prend pas de -s.

  • nombre + nom : a ten-minute break, a 200-kilometre journey, a three-year-old girl, a four-hour flight (et non a ten-minutes break)
  • adjectif + nom + -ed : a black-haired man, a blue-eyed child, a warm-hearted host
  • adjectif / adverbe + participe : a well-known poet, a fast-growing city, a Spanish-speaking island, a hand-made quilt

Compare : The flight lasts four hours. / It is a four-hour flight.

Le groupe nominal complexe

StructureEmploiExemples
N N (nom composé)catégorie, matière, fonction ; le 2e nom est le noyaua football team, a gold rush, a wind farm, a teacup
N's N (cas possessif)possession par une personne, un groupe, un lieu ; duréeCanada's largest port, a children's book, a day's work
N of Npartie, quantité, contenanta cup of tea, the end of the war, a pair of shoes

Dans un nom composé, le premier nom est au singulier : a ticket office (pas a tickets office).

Les distributifs

MotSensExemple
both (+ pluriel)les deuxBoth cities are on the Pacific coast.
either (+ singulier)l'un ou l'autre (de deux)You can take either road.
neither (+ singulier)aucun des deuxNeither city is a capital.
each (+ singulier)chaque, pris un par un (deux ou plus)Each island has its own carnival.
every (+ singulier)chaque, tous sans exception (trois ou plus)Every state has two senators.

Avec un pronom ou un déterminant : both of them, either of them, neither of us, each of the islands. Structures corrélatives : both… and, either… or, neither… nor : Neither Seattle nor Vancouver is a capital.

Wish et if only expriment un souhait irréalisable ou un regret. Le temps du verbe qui suit est décalé dans le passé.

Ce que l'on regretteStructureExemple
une situation présentewish + prétérit (were pour be)I wish I lived in Vancouver. (je n'y vis pas) / I wish I were taller.
un fait passéwish + past perfectI wish I had visited Jamaica. (je ne l'ai pas fait)
le comportement de quelqu'un (agacement, souhait de changement)wish + sb + would + BVI wish the media would talk more about Puerto Rico.
une capacitéwish + could + BVThey wish they could vote for the president.

If only a le même sens, en plus fort : If only they had listened! If only I had more time!

Préférences : would rather

  • I'd rather (would rather) + BV : je préférerais : I'd rather stay in Seattle.
  • I'd rather + sujet + prétérit : je préférerais que quelqu'un… : I'd rather you came with us.
Attention

Pour un souhait réalisable, on n'emploie pas wish mais hope : I hope you have a good trip (et non I wish you have). Mais on dit I wish you a good trip (nom complément) et I wish to + BV dans une langue soutenue (= I want to).

sections.titre: Grammar: How questions, question tags, short answers
sections.html:
Les questions en How

QuestionPorte surExemple
How often…?la fréquenceHow often do ferries leave? Every hour.
How many times…?le nombre de foisHow many times have you been there? Twice.
How long…?la durée ; la longueurHow long does the trip take? About three hours.
How far…?la distanceHow far is Seattle from Vancouver? About 200 km.
How much / How many…?la quantité (indénombrable / dénombrable), le prixHow much does a ticket cost? How many people live there?
How tall / high / wide / deep / old…?la mesure, l'âgeHow tall is the Space Needle? How old is the city?
How well…?le degré, la qualitéHow well do you speak Spanish?

Les question tags

Un tag est une petite question en fin de phrase (« n'est-ce pas ? »). On reprend l'auxiliaire de la phrase et le pronom sujet, en inversant la polarité :

  • phrase affirmative → tag négatif : Puerto Rico is a US territory, isn't it? You have been to Kingston, haven't you?
  • phrase négative → tag affirmatif : Barbados isn't a monarchy any more, is it? She can't vote, can she?
  • sans auxiliaire, on emploie do / does / did : Walcott won the Nobel Prize, didn't he? You live in Seattle, don't you?
  • cas particuliers : I am right, aren't I? Let's go, shall we? Close the door, will you?

Intonation descendante : on attend une confirmation ; montante : on pose vraiment la question.

Les réponses courtes

On répond avec le sujet pronom et l'auxiliaire, sans répéter le verbe : "Is Seattle in Canada?" "No, it isn't." "Did you see the Space Needle?" "Yes, I did." "Have they ever been to Trinidad?" "Yes, they have." Pour réagir : "I love reggae." "So do I." / "I don't like the rain." "Neither do I." / "He's never been there." "Hasn't he?"

chapitres.a_retenir:
• Les Caraïbes anglophones sont devenues indépendantes à partir de 1962 (la Barbade est une république depuis 2021) et coopèrent dans la CARICOM (1973). Leur culture rayonne (reggae, calypso, carnavals, Derek Walcott, prix Nobel 1992), mais les échanges restent inégaux (tourisme, ouragans, fuite des cerveaux).
  • Porto Rico, cédé aux États-Unis en 1898, est un Commonwealth depuis 1952 ; ses habitants sont citoyens américains depuis 1917, mais ne votent pas à l'élection présidentielle sur l'île. Le débat oppose statut actuel, 51e État et indépendance ; seul le Congrès peut admettre un nouvel État.
  • Vancouver et Seattle, à environ 200 km l'une de l'autre, forment la région de Cascadia : coopération (Peace Arch, technologie) et rivalité, avec l'attraction des salaires américains.
  • Adjectifs composés invariables (a ten-minute break) ; noms composés (a wind farm), cas possessif (Canada's largest port), N of N ; both + pluriel, either / neither / each / every + singulier.
  • wish + prétérit (regret présent), + past perfect (regret passé), + would (souhait de changement) ; if only ; I'd rather.
  • Questions en How (often, long, far, much, many, tall) ; tags : auxiliaire + pronom, polarité inversée (isn't it?, didn't he?) ; réponses courtes (Yes, I did. So do I.).
